Reading his letter again while composing her reply softened her feelings so much that Emma had to strengthen her resolve with a few firm remarks. She was so distressed at the thought of making him unhappy, so concerned about what his mother and sisters would say and think, and so anxious not to seem ungrateful that Emma believed she would still have accepted him if he had appeared just then.

Nevertheless, the reply was written, sealed, and sent. The matter was settled, and Harriet was safe. She remained rather subdued all evening, but Emma understood her kindly regrets. Sometimes she eased them by assuring Harriet of her own affection, and sometimes by bringing up Mr. Elton.

“I’ll never be invited to Abbey-Mill again,” Harriet said rather sadly.

“And even if you were, my dear Harriet, I could never bear to let you go. We need you far too much at Hartfield to spare you for Abbey-Mill.”

“I’m sure I would never want to go. Hartfield is the only place where I’m happy.”

A little later she said, “I think Mrs. Goddard would be very surprised if she knew what had happened. Miss Nash certainly would. She thinks her own sister married very well, and her husband only sells linen.”

“We could hardly wish a schoolteacher to have greater pride or refinement, Harriet. I’m sure Miss Nash would envy you this chance to marry. Even this admirer would seem valuable to her. As for your prospects of something better, I imagine she knows nothing. A certain person’s attentions can scarcely have become Highbury gossip yet. So far, I think you and I are the only ones who understand what his looks and behavior mean.”

Harriet blushed, smiled, and said something about being amazed that people liked her so much. Thinking of Mr. Elton certainly lifted her spirits. Before long, though, she began feeling tender concern again for the rejected Mr. Martin.

“He must have my letter now,” she said quietly. “I wonder what they’re all doing, whether his sisters know. If he’s unhappy, they’ll be unhappy too. I hope he won’t take it too badly.”

“Let’s think instead of our absent friends who are doing something happier,” Emma exclaimed. “Perhaps this very moment Mr. Elton is showing your portrait to his mother and sisters, explaining how much more beautiful you are in person. And after they have asked five or six times, perhaps he is finally letting them hear your name, your own dear name.”

“If I can’t live on that, I won’t ask anyone to help me out. Is that acceptable?”

An enormous roar of applause followed. Above it rose the king’s voice:

“Remove his chains and release him! Everyone, high and low, rich and poor, pay him honor. He is now the king’s right hand, invested with power and authority, and his place is on the throne’s highest step. Now banish this creeping darkness and restore the light and joy, so the whole world may bless you.”

But I said:

“For an ordinary man to be humiliated before the world is nothing. But it would dishonor the king if those who saw his minister naked did not also see his dignity restored. If I could ask for my clothes to be brought back—”

“They are unsuitable,” the king interrupted. “Bring different clothing. Dress him like a prince!”

My idea worked. I needed to leave things as they were until the eclipse became total. Otherwise, they would keep demanding that I remove the darkness, which of course I couldn’t do. Fetching clothes bought some time, but not enough, so I needed another excuse. I said the king might naturally change his mind and regret some of the decisions he had made in his excitement. Therefore, I would let the darkness deepen for a while. If, after a reasonable interval, his decision remained unchanged, I would dismiss it. Neither the king nor anyone else liked that arrangement, but I had to insist.

The sky grew darker and blacker as I wrestled with those awkward sixth-century clothes. Finally, everything went pitch-black. The crowd groaned in terror as cold, eerie night breezes swept through the place and stars appeared, twinkling overhead. At last the eclipse was complete. I was delighted, though everyone else was miserable, which was understandable. I said:

“By remaining silent, the king confirms that he accepts the terms.” Then I raised my hands, held the pose for a moment, and declared with the most terrifying solemnity, “Let the spell dissolve and disappear without causing harm!”

For a moment nothing answered in that deep darkness and graveyard silence. Then, a moment or two later, the sun’s silver edge emerged. The crowd erupted in a tremendous shout and surged toward me like a flood, overwhelming me with blessings and gratitude. Clarence, you can be sure, was nowhere near the back of that wave.

Mr. Darcy praised his sister’s skill with affection.

“I am very pleased to hear she is doing so well,” Lady Catherine said. “Please tell her from me that she cannot expect to excel unless she practices a great deal.”

“I assure you, madam,” he replied, “she needs no such advice. She practices all the time.”

“So much the better. One cannot practice too much. The next time I write, I will insist that she never neglect it. I often tell young women that excellence in music requires constant practice. I have told Miss Bennet several times that she will never play really well unless she practices more. Mrs. Collins may have no instrument, but, as I have often said, Miss Bennet is perfectly welcome to come to Rosings every day and use the piano in Mrs. Jenkinson’s room. In that part of the house, you see, she would be in nobody’s way.”

Mr. Darcy looked slightly embarrassed by his aunt’s bad manners and said nothing.

After coffee, Colonel Fitzwilliam reminded Elizabeth that she had promised to play for him. She immediately sat at the piano, and he pulled a chair close to her. Lady Catherine listened to half a song before resuming her conversation with her other nephew. Eventually he left her and approached the piano with his usual unhurried manner. He stood where he could see the attractive performer’s face clearly. Elizabeth noticed, and at the first suitable pause she turned to him with a playful smile.

“You mean to frighten me, Mr. Darcy, by coming over so grandly to listen. But I refuse to be intimidated, even if your sister does play beautifully. I have a stubborn streak that will never allow people to frighten me simply because they choose to. Every attempt to intimidate me only increases my courage.”

“I won’t say you are mistaken,” he replied, “because you cannot seriously believe I intend to frighten you. Besides, I have known you long enough to realize how much you sometimes enjoy expressing opinions you don’t actually hold.”

Elizabeth laughed heartily at this description and turned to Colonel Fitzwilliam. “Your cousin will give you a lovely impression of me and teach you to distrust everything I say. How unlucky I am to meet someone so capable of revealing my true character, in a place where I hoped to pass myself off with a reasonably good reputation.
